paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: By the beginning of the 20th century, thanks to rapid industrialisation, a growing economy, and a diverse climate, the United States had established a culture of informal dressing amongst men that set it apart from Europe. The USA had its own sporting interests in baseball and American football, which contributed to uniquely American expressions in men's leisurewear and sportswear. Baseball jackets, colourful Hawaiian shirts, and lumber jackets had no equivalents elsewhere. Moreover, North American men were more receptive to the notions of comfort and ease than, for example, their European counterparts. North America therefore took on the role of leisurewear pioneer, embracing it as its own.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In the 1950s, variations of the short-sleeved T-shirt worn by North American servicemen began to appear in army surplus stores and in the movies, which did much to redefine the former undergarment into an item with wider appeal. T-shirts have subsequently been customised by individual wearers over the years, representing an attachment to a particular style, brand, or community, and have become an ever-popular favourite of male peer groups and counter-culture dressing. They have also been transformed into a political item of dress, featuring a variety of controversial slogans and eye-catching images, as well as taking on the role of the classic tourist souvenir, with amusing sayings and memorable pictures from innumerable locations.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Denim jeans mirrored this development, beginning life as workwear in the mid-19th-century Californian gold rush. The canvas trousers created by immigrant Levi Strauss were well received by the miners, but the stiff fabric was uncomfortable so it was replaced with a cotton fabric from France known as denim. In the years following the gold rush, jeans gradually established themselves as practical workwear garments for North America's farmers and blue-collar workers. During the 1930s, it was said that east coast visitors to the former 'wild west' returned home with a pair of jeans as a memento of their visit, introducing them to a receptive new audience, but also fuelling the growing myth that associated denim jeans with the early cowboy culture of the west. In reality, they were adopted by cowboys as late as the 1890s; nevertheless, they became inextricably linked to the spirit of adventure and freedom. When screen and music stars including Marlon Brando and Elvis Presley were seen wearing jeans in the 1950s, their cult standing was confirmed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Men's designer jeans were introduced in Europe and North America in the late 1970s, in a move which represented unknown territory for some manufacturers. The dilemma for the men's jeans market was that the notion of 'designer' flew in the face of the garment's original appeal as an item of nonconformity and youthful expression. Within a few years and in response to street styles that encouraged customisation, such as the adding of tears and rips, manufacturers replicated these looks and re-marketed jeans to a more informed public. In effect, designer jeans became streetwise.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The history and evolution of men's leisurewear, and in particular sportswear, during the 20th century is closely associated with the development of synthetic materials. Hailed as a 'miracle fibre' when it was commercially introduced in 1939, nylon went on to become one of the most widely used synthetic polymers of the second half of the 20th century. It was made from petrochemicals and established the basis for other manufactured fibres. These were used to create garments that were practical and durable, which meant they were stronger and more hard-wearing than clothes made from natural fibres. During the late 1940s and 1950s, clothing manufacturers began to identify opportunities for applying synthetic materials to sportswear. Simple and efficient production systems, making ready-to-wear items, were well established by the mid-20th century, and were extremely compatible with the new synthetic materials.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The second half of the 20th century witnessed the transformation of sportswear, from clothing that was worn almost exclusively by professional athletes, to branded clothing and accessories worn by wider sections of society. The impact of sportswear on menswear during the closing decades of the 20th century was revolutionary. With its close associations to physical performance and health, sportswear attracted new generations of men who sought to break with the restrictive dress styles of their fathers and grandfathers. The post-war ascent of sportswear coincided with the rise of the teenager and the phenomenon of youth-orientated pop culture across Europe and North America.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Of course, sportswear was never going to replace all modes of male dress and has had no real impact on formal wear, but its large-scale adoption around the world today has made it a potent force in menswear. Some sociologists would argue that sportswear has succeeded in replacing one uniform way of dressing with another. Certainly, the expansion and popularity of sportswear has made it appear ubiquitous. Manufacturers have come to recognise the importance of ongoing investment in manufacturing processes and effective brand communication as necessities for continued expansion and success. Therefore, high-profile branding and a signature logo have become an integral and indispensable part of men's sportswear and accessories. The sector now represents a multi-billion dollar global industry in which individual sportswear companies are driven by the momentum to stay one step ahead of the competition: other sportswear firms.
